cover.hook:
Why does tennis
look faster live?
cover.subject: Courtside vs TV
cover.topic: Angular speed, camera angle and window

push.lead: The same 200 km/h serve sweeps about 138° a second across your view courtside, but only about 19° on TV. The broadcast camera squashes the court's depth, and our eyes are less sensitive to motion in depth. Football is the other way round: the stands show the whole pitch, so the ball looks slower.

editorial.question: Why does tennis look faster live than on TV, while football looks faster on TV?
editorial.thesis: The brain judges speed by the angle an object sweeps across the retina per second, not by its physical speed. Tennis's main TV camera sits high behind the baseline, so the ball mostly travels in depth: a small angular speed, and depth motion is detected less sensitively. Courtside, the ball sweeps sideways, far beyond the smooth-pursuit limit. Football is the reverse: the stands show the whole 105 m pitch, TV frames only about 40 m, and by Brown's window effect the same speed looks slower in a bigger window.
beats: Puzzle: tennis looks faster live, football looks faster on TV
How fast: a 200 km/h serve lands in ~0.4 s and reaches the returner in ~0.7 s
Camera: high behind the baseline, tilted ~12° down; depth is squashed
Angular speed: courtside ~138°/s vs TV ~19°/s, about 7×
Eyes: smooth pursuit tops out ~70°/s; depth-motion sensitivity ~1/3 of sideways
Window: Brown 1931, a 2× window needs ~1.94× the speed to look as fast
Real life: through a screen, other people's rallies look easy
sources: J.F. Brown (1931). The visual perception of velocity. Psychologische Forschung 14:199–232
H. Wallach (1939). On constancy of visual speed. Psychological Review 46:541–552
C.W. Tyler (1971). Stereoscopic depth movement: two eyes less sensitive than one. Science 174:958–961
Meyer, Lasker & Robinson (1985). The upper limit of human smooth pursuit velocity. Vision Research 25:561–563
Regan & Gray (2000). Visually guided collision avoidance and collision achievement. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4:99–107
ATP 250 TV Production Manual (2023): Camera 1 sightline
David Foster Wallace (2006). Federer as Religious Experience. The New York Times
editorial._assumptions: Angular speeds and serve times are simplified-model estimates; camera distance, seats and screen size are illustrative assumptions (stated on the references card).
